item.title: Pathological Periodicity, Part III: The Periodic Decomposition Problem and Vitali sets.
item.dc:creator: Alonso Espinosa Domínguez
item.description:
This is Part III of the series Pathological Periodicity. The previous installment is Part II: The Cage of Continuity; start from the beginning with Part I: Relearning the Basics.

Introduction

It has been 5 months since my last post. I did not intend for there to be such a substantial gap between installments, but a handful of things have gotten in the way of my writing. For one, the list of deeply interrelated questions vying for center stage in Pathological Periodicity has grown without bound; naturally, I ended up pursuing too many of these simultaneously, making it difficult to finish writing about any of them. On top of that, several months back I began to learn about a totally distinct topic in 3-D algebraic topology, prompted by a former professor of mine. It was perhaps a bit over-ambitious to try to handle both projects at once given my other time constraints, but oh well, I guess I can’t help but learn these things the hard way still.

Anyhow, my thoughts on what to emphasize in this series and how to organize it have naturally changed over the last few months. I had originally planned to hold off on a detailed discussion of the Periodic Decomposition Problem, which I informally introduced in Part I, until a later post. As such, I initially drafted this post as a discussion of the pathological examples promised at the end of Part II. But it now seems to me that the most interesting results and examples will be best appreciated after a formal introduction to this problem. That is what we will begin here.

Specifically, in this installment I will reproduce — albeit with a twist! — the classic, choice-dependent proof of a foundational result in the literature on the decomposition problem, which I have decided to call the Periodic Decomposition Theorem (PDT). Unlike the classic proof, however, the one here will allow us to conclude the PDT’s precise level of dependence on the Axiom of Choice (AC). We will see that over ZF, the PDT is equivalent to the existence of a selector for whenever is irrational, i.e. a set containing a single element from each coset in the quotient. However, assuming I am interpreting some foundational theorems in descriptive set theory correctly (despite my shaky grasp of their proofs), these selectors and thus the PDT are equivalent, over ZF, to the existence of a Vitali set — a selector for . As will be explained below, the existence of Vitali sets is one of many famous examples of a weak choice principle: a statement that follows from AC but is strictly weaker than it (and not provable in ZF).

In fact, the equivalence sharpens in a way I find wonderful. The PDT gives the necessary and sufficient condition for any function in to decompose into a sum of any finite number of periodic summands. And yet what turns out to be equivalent to all of it (and to the existence of a Vitali set) is the existence of just one single decomposition of one single function: writing as the sum of a function with period and a function with period .

Let me begin with some basic background on the periodic decomposition problem, and formally state the PDT. In the next section, I will be borrowing from a survey of this problem by the Hungarian mathematicians Bálint Farkas and Szilárd Gy. Révész.1 Let’s jump in.

Remark. Before we begin: this post builds directly on the terminology and notation set up earlier in the series. In particular I will write for the period group of — the subgroup of consisting of all of its periods — and for the difference operator . Both are introduced in Part II: The Cage of Continuity, along with the basic facts about period groups that I will use without comment. If anything below looks unfamiliar, that is the place to look.

The Periodic Decomposition Problem

The periodic decomposition problem begins with the observation that if a function can be written as

Thus, Equation 2 is a necessary condition for to be decomposable in this manner. The decomposition problem, which goes back at least to the 1970s in Hungary, consists of determining when the implication can be reversed.2 This is a nice generalization of the fact that a function is periodic with period if and only if .

It will help to have a name for the thing being asked about. I will say that admits a -decomposition if it can be written as in Equation 1 with for each . Note that nothing in this definition requires the to be incommensurable (i.e. ), nor the summands to be anything more than periodic. Finer distinctions along these lines will matter in the next post; here the plain notion is all we need.

Notice that the identity always satisfies Equation 2 (for ) no matter which we choose. But if the are all commensurable,3 the intersection contains some nonzero number . This means it cannot be the case that has a decomposition of the form Equation 1, for in that case the sum on the right-hand side of Equation 1 would be periodic with period , and has no periods other than . However, for a system of pairwise incommensurable real numbers , we do have the following theorem assuming the Axiom of Choice, which I will refer to as the Periodic Decomposition Theorem (PDT).

Theorem 1 (Periodic Decomposition Theorem) Let be pairwise incommensurable. Then a function admits a -decomposition if and only if Equation 2 holds.

This appears to have been first proved by the Italian analysts Stefano Mortola and Roberto Peirone in 1999 (20+ years after the decomposition problem was first posed), and has been the point of departure for much work on this problem since then.4

Mortola and Peirone tackle the problem assuming the existence of a basis for as a -vector space — a Hamel basis. Later we will see that this is one of the famous weak choice principles, sitting, in terms of deductive strength, between the existence of a Vitali set and the existence of a well-ordering of the reals.

The motivating insight is that, granted such a basis, it is easy to decompose into a sum of two periodic functions. Write for the basis, so that every real has a unique expansion

with all but finitely many equal to zero. Pick two distinct indices and split the expansion in two:

Adding to bumps the coordinate by one and leaves every other coordinate alone, so does not notice: . Adding leaves alone, so . And of course . So , a function with no nonzero period whatsoever, is the sum of two periodic functions.

Mortola and Peirone realized this could be pushed a great deal further: a more sophisticated version of the same Hamel-basis maneuver decomposes not just , but any satisfying Equation 2 for any system of pairwise-incommensurable periods . All of the work is concentrated into a single lemma:

Lemma 1 (Mortola–Peirone) Let be incommensurable, and let be -periodic. Then there exists a -periodic such that .

Said differently: the operator , restricted to the space of -periodic functions, maps that space onto itself. After we discuss some set-theoretic preliminaries, we will give a proof that closely resembles theirs but replaces the Hamel basis with the weaker assumption that there exists a selector for for at least one pair such that (and we will describe why this in turn should reduce to the assumption that a vitali set exists).

For now, let’s proceed to the proof of the PDT that follows once the lemma is in hand.

Proof. Necessity is the observation we opened with, so only sufficiency is at issue. We argue by induction on .

For , the hypothesis says exactly that is -periodic, so is already a decomposition.

Suppose the theorem holds for , and let be pairwise incommensurable with meaning the inductive hypothesis applies to the function : there are with and Each is -periodic, and is incommensurable with , so Lemma 1 applies to the pair : there is a -periodic with . Put . Since is linear, and therefore . That is, is -periodic, and is a decomposition of the required form.

That is the entire proof. What makes it go is that Lemma 1 lets us lift a decomposition of to a decomposition of itself. Its a neat little proof.

Needless to say, I was very excited to find Mortola and Peirone’s paper. Months ago I tried to prove the PDT by exactly this induction, but I got as far as reducing the whole problem to the need for Lemma 1 and then simply could not produce it. I knew Mortola and Peirone had proved it and I suspected they probably did so via a similar route, but somehow I failed to find a pdf of their paper at the time. As such, an earlier draft of this post contained proofs of weaker versions of the PDT that I was able to prove on my own. Those I could show were equivalent to existence of a Vitali set, but I was very dissatisfied not being able to say for sure whether the PDT in general was. So I am quite happy to have finally found a copy of the paper, even though it forced me to rewrite a good chunk of this post.

And the rewrite was well worth it, for the following reason. Notice where the Axiom of Choice appears in the induction argument above: nowhere! It is pure ZF. All of the choice consumed by the PDT is consumed inside Lemma 1. So the question of how much choice the PDT needs reduces entirely to the question of how much choice that one lemma needs. To make sense of this, let’s review some set theory.

A little set theory

For the last 100 years, set theory has acted as the de facto foundation for most of mathematics. The majority of mathematicians use set theory fairly informally; they know set theorists have worked out all kinds of axiomatic systems to justify their manipulations with sets, and that the system called “Zermelo–Fraenkel Set Theory with the Axiom of Choice (ZFC)” in particular seems to work well for most of their purposes. But they often don’t concern themselves too much with the details of these axioms. In these posts, we will still use set theory relatively informally, but we will concern ourselves heavily with the exact dependence of statements on the Axiom of Choice.

Recall that the Axiom of Choice (AC) states that given any family of nonempty sets , there exists a choice function or selector on such that for all . AC is equivalent to a great many other statements, including the Well-Ordering Theorem (every set can be well-ordered) and the assertion that every vector space has a basis.

Whenever is pairwise disjoint, which is the only case we will care about, notice that a choice function exists iff there exists a set so that contains a single element for every . Such a set is also called a selector by some, in a harmless abuse of terminology. Others call it a transversal. I will generally use selector.

AC in full generality is quite powerful, but when applied in practice you often don’t need to actually assume that literally any family as above has a choice function. You just need to assume that one exists for the kinds of family you are actually working with; or perhaps that a basis exists for the specific vector spaces you are interested in; or that a particular set can be well-ordered; etc.

If you are working with finite families of sets, you don’t even need an additional axiom. Finite choice, as it is called, can be proved from the axioms of ZF alone. Once the family is infinite, however, ZF alone no longer guarantees you a choice function. Sometimes you can still write one down by hand — if every member of the family happens to be a nonempty set of natural numbers, just take the least element of each — but in general you cannot, and asserting that you can means adding an axiom to your underlying set theory. A statement that follows from the Axiom of Choice but is neither equivalent to it nor provable in ZF is what I will call a weak choice principle. Examples include the Axiom of Countable Choice,5 and the Axiom of Dependent Choice (DC), which we will meet shortly. But the two principles we care about most in this series are the assertion that there exists a Vitali set (call this assertion VIT for brevity), and the assertion that there is a Hamel basis (call this HB).

Recall that a Vitali set is a selector for , so that VIT is the assertion that such a selector exists. This makes it as restricted a form of AC as one could ask for: it is the single instance of AC applied to the family of cosets of . In addition to this, Vitali sets are famous as the quintessential (non-constructive) examples of nonmeasurable subsets of the real line.

Meanwhile HB also seems to be nearly as restrictive a form of AC as VIT. After all, AC is equivalent to the statement that every vector space has a basis, and asserting a Hamel basis cuts this down to the single vector space over .

VIT and HB, however, are not equally weak. According to recent research, over ZF, granting a Hamel basis yields a Vitali set, a well-ordering of yields a Hamel basis, and of course AC yields any and all of these.

That a Hamel basis yields a Vitali set is not hard to see and has been long known. First, take your existing basis and get a new basis containing (replace any basis element in the expansion for with ). Then the -span of is a complementary subspace to in , and hence a selector for .6 The converses are another matter entirely. That ZF + HB does not imply a well-ordering of the reals is a theorem published in 2018, and that ZF + VIT does not imply HB is proved in a 2020 book under a large-cardinal assumption, though a preprint from two months ago (June 2026!) claims this assumption can be dropped.7

To be clear, VIT is still stronger than what can be proved in ZF alone. The famous witness to this is the Solovay model, a model of ZF + DC in which all subsets of the real line are Lebesgue measurable, so that no Vitali set can exist in it.8 Saharon Shelah later built a different model of ZF + DC which likewise contains no Vitali set, and whose consistency rests on nothing beyond the consistency of ZF.9 So we can say with confidence that VIT is independent of ZF, provided ZF is consistent at all.

So where does this leave the PDT? As we saw, Mortola and Peirone’s argument only uses AC in Lemma 1, and does so by assuming the existence of a Hamel basis. The proof we will give in the next section needs only selectors for quotients of the form , for all pairs with . But a selector for is not literally a Vitali set: is not . So the question naturally arises: over ZF, what does the existence of a selector for a quotient by one subgroup of imply about the existence of one for another, and in particular for ?

Transferability of selectors and Borel equivalence relations

It will be helpful now to recast these quotients in terms of equivalence relations. For a countable additive subgroup , let be the equivalence relation . The equivalence classes of are of course the cosets in . I.e. . This relation moreover is Borel and countable (every equivalence class is a countable set). Leaning on the theory of countable Borel equivalence relations, I claim the following proposition:

Proposition 1 Let and let . Over ZF, a selector for exists if and only if a selector for exists.

This may look trivial, but the “over ZF” has made it actually quite challenging to prove; the naive proof one is tempted to try uses a lot of choice. And unfortunately, there does not seem to be any published work stating this proposition exactly. Nonetheless I am convinced that, at worst, Proposition 1 is a special case of well-established, if highly technical, results in descriptive set theory that are choice-free at least when applied to this specific statement. At best, I might be able to sidestep the heavy machinery to give a more elementary (if still non-obvious) proof inspired by one I found from 1975 that shows you can “transfer” selectors in the case of and .

Tracing the relevant literature, the extent to which it uses AC, and attempting an elementary proof has turned into a separate post I am writing and hoping to publish soon. For now, I will give an extremely condensed preview of the literature that justifies asserting Proposition 1, leaving all definitions and detailed citations for the later post.

Again let . Then the countable Borel relations and are both examples in ZF of hyperfinite, nonsmooth equivalence relations; though showing hyperfiniteness for is less straightforward than for . One of the classic theorems in descriptive set theory is that any two countable hyperfinite, nonsmooth relations are bi-embeddable (see this paper). In turn, for any countable subgroups , ZF proves that if and are bi-embeddable, then a selector for one exists iff a selector for the other exists. This last assertion is the one relatively easy thing here to prove outright in ZF: given an injection such that and a selector for , one can write down a selector for by an explicit formula, using a fixed enumeration of to pick canonical representatives. I will give the construction in the follow-up post.

Unfortunately, it seems descriptive set theorists generally work in ZFC without paying too much attention to how much choice they do or do not use; theorems like the one on bi-embeddability were not proved with our need for choiceless results in mind. So far, the results we need seem choiceless when applied to our context, though I am still verifying this. But luckily for us, prominent set theorists Paul Larson and Jindřich Zapletal pay very careful attention to usage of choice principles, and in Discontinuous homomorphisms, selectors, and automorphisms of the complex field (in ZF) (2020), they cite the bi-embeddability theorem in asserting that a Vitali selector exists iff one exists for , all while working entirely in ZF. So for now, we will proceed assuming the relevant machinery does indeed imply Proposition 1 holds without recourse to AC.

The PDT and the existence of a Vitali set

Now we can tackle the main result of this post:

Theorem 2 (The PDT, Vitali sets, and a single decomposition) Over ZF, the following three statements are equivalent:

  1. admits a -decomposition;
  2. there exists a Vitali set;
  3. the Periodic Decomposition Theorem (Theorem 1) holds.

To prove this, we first need a proof of Lemma 1 that gets by with a selector for , as opposed to a Hamel basis. Thankfully, it turns out to be pretty easy to replace a Hamel basis with such a selector without altering their proof too much. 10 In the following, we assume the existence of this selector.

Putting now our proofs of Lemma 1 and Theorem 1 together with Proposition 1:

Proposition 2 Over ZF, VIT implies the PDT.

For the reverse direction, let me first explain the thought process that led me there. Before I knew whether any of this was true, it was evident that the PDT does imply the existence of nonmeasurable (though not necessarily Vitali) sets, and is thus independent of ZF, per Solovay. This follows because (and in fact any with ) cannot have a measurable decomposition (see the survey by Farkas and Révész), yet must have a decomposition in ZF + PDT. This suggested to me that a possible way to prove the converse is to show that a decomposition of must itself induce a Vitali-type set. I thought that maybe one of the nonmeasurable pre-images of a summand in the decomposition must actually be such a Vitali-type set.

But I was stuck on how to prove this, and I was not sure if it was even true. So I set this down for a few months while I worked on other questions. It turns out that I was most of the way there. The function is in fact the correct one to consider, and the easiest selector to find is a particular intersection of the pre-images of the summands.

The key is to see that if is a -decomposition of , then and , and thus and can occur only once per coset. To put this more formally:

Lemma 2 Suppose with , and suppose admits a -decomposition, with and . Then the set is a selector for .

Proof. Since and for every ,

and symmetrically for every , using .

Let . Then for some and , where may be zero. This means is in the same coset as , and . Similarly, for some and , and thus is in the same coset as , and . Let . Then is in the same coset as , and, since and , we have and . Thus . In other words, each coset intersects at least once.

Now we observe that this must be unique. Let be in the same coset. Then for some . But then and . Since and , we must have , and thus . Therefore, each coset intersects at most once. This finishes the proof that is a selector for .

A perfectly simple, elementary proof that eluded me for months! And with it we can close the circle and prove Theorem 2:

Proof. (1) (2). Given with and , Lemma 2 turns the decomposition into a selector for , and Proposition 1 turns that selector into a Vitali set.

(2) (3). This is Proposition 2.

(3) (1). Immediate: as we observed at the outset, , and , so the PDT applies to with this pair.

The argument runs verbatim for any positive, incommensurable and , not just with and , but this is a particularly “cute” pair to use. After all, the term “incommensurable” comes from the Latin translation for the Greek asúmmetros which Euclid used for pairs of lengths with irrational ratios, and the first such pair they discovered was the diagonal and side of a unit square. Anyhow, all of these single-pair statements — that has a -decomposition, that it has a -decomposition, that it has a -decomposition — are equivalent to one another, and each of them is equivalent to the PDT in full.

To me, this is pretty neat. Statement (3) quantifies over every real function and every finite system of periods while statement (1) asks for a single decomposition of a single specific function along a single specific pair of numbers. You wouldn’t necessarily expect these two statements to be equivalent to each other and to a famous weak choice principle.

But this is only the beginning. There are many possible variations of the PDT that can be considered by altering the conditions on the summands in the decomposition. We could also generalize beyond periodicity by considering operators on arbitrary sets and -invariance of functions defined by ; this is actually the route taken by Farkas and Révész in the 2007 paper mentioned above, where the PDT falls out as a corollary of a more general “invariant decomposition” theorem.11 In each such variation or generalization, we can ask what choice principles the resulting decomposition theorems require or are equivalent to. I’ll be writing more about this in the future.

Conclusion

Here is why we should care about all this: AC is very powerful when it comes to proving that things exist. Indeed, in some ways, it is a little too powerful: AC together with the rest of ZF can be used to assert the existence of objects that are impossible to explicitly construct, and some of these are very bizarre (as Pathological Periodicity will attest to). This seems to be one of many factors that push a (fairly small) minority of mathematicians to reject ZFC as an axiom system.

I don’t think it is necessary to reject ZFC outright. I do think however that figuring out precisely how much various proofs throughout “standard” mathematics depend on AC and on weaker choice principles is in and of itself highly interesting and worthwhile mathematics. Doing so gives us a more accurate picture of the spectrum of deductive strength held by results that are provable in ZFC, and of how far the objects ZFC proves as exist sit from anything you could explicitly construct.

Philosophically, I think this matters because, even if you accept the existence of mathematical objects that cannot be explicitly constructed, such objects come with domains of applicability that differ considerably from others. Grant a Hamel basis, for instance, and there exist -linear functions that fail to be -linear. These are quite pathological: they are nowhere continuous, their graphs are dense in the plane, and they are nonmeasurable. But you will never write one down, never evaluate one at a point, never compute anything with one. Nor will you do so with the summands of any periodic decomposition of . Their existence is a fact about what ZFC can prove that is beyond the reach of ZF, not a fact you can put to work to model the motion of a ball or the behavior of a quantum system. Locating a theorem on the spectrum above means knowing, for that theorem, roughly how much it depends on objects whose relationship to the rest of material reality is distinctly indirect.

A good chunk of Pathological Periodicity will be about parsing out this spectrum specifically within the literature on the Periodic Decomposition Problem. Today, we got a nice start by pinning down the PDT exactly. Throughout the rest of the series, we will seek to pin down the deductive strength of other variants of the PDT, as well as that of some of the highly pathological phenomena that arise amongst functions admitting a periodic decomposition.12

Two periodic functions and are incommensurable if they share no period other than , that is, if , and commensurable otherwise. The two notions are related but not interchangeable: if and are incommensurable functions, then any nonzero period of one is incommensurable with any nonzero period of the other. Knowing that any one period of is incommensurable with a period of however does not allow you to conclude the functions are incommensurable.↩︎

As a little preview: assuming a selector for a particular quotient of involving an uncountable subgroup, there exist whole vector subspaces of consisting entirely of periodic functions, and yet generated by 2 or more pairwise incommensurable functions (this answers Question 4 of Part I). It is unclear to me as of yet where the existence of this selector sits among the weak choice principles relative to VIT, and whether the existence of such subspaces implies the existence of the selector. The two-dimensional case is prototypical. It already takes a bit of creativity to find incommensurable periodic and with periodic sum; ensuring is periodic for every single is considerably harder, and is what requires more choice than is available in ZF. The first post I write on this will probably confine itself to the two-dimensional case over . I have been working on pushing it further — to more general function spaces over other fields, and possibly to an uncountable-dimensional subspace of with the same property — but I am still working out the details.↩︎

item.title: Pathological Periodicity, Part II: The Cage of Continuity
item.dc:creator: Alonso Espinosa Domínguez
item.description:
This is Part II of the series Pathological Periodicity. Start from the beginning with Part I: Relearning the Basics.

Introduction and Preliminaries1

In the previous post, I motivated a series of questions surrounding the sums of periodic functions and the existence of functions with incommensurable periods. Now, we are ready to dive in. We will see that many of the things we intuitively hold to be true (or that I at least held to be true) about periodic functions do indeed hold for continuous functions in particular. We will also start to see, however, that the structural richness of sets of periods leaves much room for pathological behavior deviating starkly from intuitions based on the continuous functions.

To begin, I’ll review the basic definitions and facts about periodic functions that set the stage for our further explorations, revealing the interplay of algebra and topology in the world of periodicity.

Definition 1 (Periodic Function) A function is said to be periodic if there exists a non-zero real number such that for all . If there exists a smallest positive such , it is called the fundamental period of , and we say is strictly periodic.

Remark. Note that a function can be periodic without being strictly periodic; for instance, the constant functions are trivially periodic (every number is a period), but they are not strictly periodic. As we will see below, the constant functions are far from the only example.

Definition 2 (The Period Group) For any function , we denote by the set of all periods of , i.e., . We call the period group of . Also, we say two periodic functions and are incommensurable if , and they are commensurable otherwise.

(Note: Constant functions are trivially commensurable with any periodic function. Non-periodic functions still have a period group, but it is just .)

Also, we say “period group” because this set is literally a group (a subgroup of ) with respect to addition: for any , the set is closed under all finite integer linear combinations, as is easily verified. In other words, whenever and are integers and . For anyone unfamiliar with group theory: generally whenever we say some subset is an (additive) group, we will mean it is closed with respect to finite integer linear combinations.

A few more basic and useful facts that follow from these definitions:

  • Fact 1: Two functions are incommensurable to each other if and only if each nonzero period of is incommensurable to every nonzero period of , meaning their ratio is irrational (hence why we use this terminology for functions as well as numbers). Equivalently, the functions are commensurable iff there exist nonzero numbers and that are commensurable (). This holds because iff there exist nonzero integers such that , and thus , showing that and are commensurable functions per our earlier definition.
  • Fact 2: Clearly if a function’s period group is cyclic and nontrivial, meaning for some number , then is strictly periodic with fundamental period . Actually, we can sharpen this: is strictly periodic if and only if its period group is nontrivial and cyclic. Where is the fundamental period for a strictly periodic , the inclusion is obvious. The other inclusion is established as follows: if , there is a greatest integer so that . But then , and must be a period since is a group. Because is the fundamental period, must be therefore be identically so that .
  • Fact 3: If , and contains any half-open interval with length equal to , then is equal to the full range of . This is because for all integers , and .

Finally, recall that we say a set is dense if its closure is the whole real line. Equivalently, it is dense if every open interval contains at least one point of (which in fact guarantees every interval contains infinitely many points of ).

With these preliminary facts and definitions out of the way, we can start to see how closely the nature of a periodic function relates to the topological properties of its period group.

Proposition 1 Let be any function. If is dense, then is either constant or else it is nowhere continuous.

Proof. Suppose is not constant, let , and fix some such that is in the range of . For each integer let and . The density of guarantees the existence of periods such that . Since is a group, the difference is also a period. The interval has length exactly . Consequently by Fact 3, the image of under is the entire range of , guaranteeing there is some such that . We have therefore constructed a sequence converging to such that for all , meaning cannot be continuous at .

Proposition 2 Let be periodic. Then is dense if and only if is not strictly periodic. Thus, if a periodic is non-constant and continuous, it must be strictly periodic.

Proof. If is dense, then the infimum of positive periods must be zero (because every interval would have to contain a period of ), and thus no fundamental period can exist.

Conversely, if no fundamental period exists and , the infimum of positive periods must be zero; for otherwise, we could find two distinct periods arbitrarily close to such that their positive difference would be a positive period smaller than , violating the infimum. Thus, any interval around must contain nonzero elements of .

Now take any interval with . By the foregoing, we can find a nonzero with . There thus must be some integer so that , for otherwise we could find an so that , which contradicts . But , showing is dense in . The last part is an immediate consequence of this density and Proposition 1.

Actually, this last proposition is not even really about periodic functions specifically; it is a general fact about subgroups of , as the following corollary makes clear:

Corollary 1 Suppose is an additive subgroup of . Then is dense if and only if it is not cyclic.

Proof. If , it is cyclic and not dense, so there is nothing to prove. Otherwise, let be the characteristic function of (equal to on , zero elsewhere). Then as the reader can quickly verify, so is periodic, and Proposition 2 together with Fact 2 gives us this corollary. (We of course could have proved this first and then Proposition 2)

We see then how analytic facts about the set of continuity points of a real function frequently correspond to topological facts about the subgroups of . We add one more corollary that brings out this correspondence:

Corollary 2 Suppose is an additive subgroup of containing at least two nonzero numbers that are incommensurable. Then is dense. Therefore, any non-constant function with 2 or more incommensurable periods is nowhere continuous.

Proof. Clearly such a cannot be cyclic, and hence is dense by Corollary 1, because all nonzero elements of a cyclic group are commensurable with each other (they are of form for integers and ). The second part of the corollary then follows immediately from the first part and from Proposition 1, applied to .

The Difference Operator and Periodic Sums

Now, we revisit the question of sums of incommensurable functions, and in particular we show that in the continuous case, such sums are never periodic.

For this and for the future posts in this series, we introduce the following operator which is ubiquitously used in discussions of the periodic decomposition problem:

Definition 3 (Difference Operator) For any function and any , we define the difference operator in p by for all . As the reader can verify, these are linear operators for all , and they commute with each other, i.e., for all .

This operator measures how much changes when we translate by . In particular, is identically zero if and only if is a period of . A few more key facts about difference operators and sums of functions:

  • For any and any , we have . That is, all periods of are also periods of .
  • Given two functions , their sum is periodic if and only if there is an such that . Such an is then a period of .
  • Thus, if is a period of , then for all and all we have: which implies:
  • Hence, if is periodic, then and are commensurable for all and all , even if and are incommensurable. This however is not a sufficient condition for to be periodic, as the reader can verify (we will also see this in a later post).
  • When are incommensurable and their sum is periodic, then the above must be incommensurable with all periods of and . In other words, we actually have that for all and ,
  • If are themselves periodic and incommensurable with periodic, Equation 2 implies and each contain a pair of incommensurable elements (any nonzero element of , resp. , together with any nonzero element of ), and are therefore dense by Corollary 2, forcing and to be either constant or nowhere continuous by Proposition 1.

This leads us to the main result of this section:

Theorem 1 (The Cage of Continuity) Let be a continuous periodic function, and let be any other periodic function. Then is periodic if and only if are commensurable.

Proof. Commensurability of trivially implies periodicity of . For the other direction, suppose is periodic and are incommensurable periodic functions. We prove that neither nor could be continuous. By the discussion above, has a dense period group for any nonzero , and thus is either nowhere continuous or is a nonzero constant (since by assumption). If is nowhere continuous, then must not have been continuous to begin with. If it is a nonzero constant , then must be unbounded, because in this case , which goes to infinity as . But continuous periodic functions must be bounded, so cannot be continuous. Reasoning in the exact same way establishes non-continuity of and this finishes the proof.

The reader may wonder whether Theorem 1 can be strengthened: must incommensurable periodic functions with a periodic sum be not just discontinuous, but nowhere continuous? I initially believed so — after all, the proof above shows that and are either nowhere continuous or a nonzero constant. In the latter case, if, say, is a nonzero constant, then must in fact be nowhere bounded, which is even worse than nowhere continuous (see Exercise 1 below). In the remaining case, where is nowhere continuous, it might seem like this should force to be nowhere continuous as well. But as Exercise 2 shows, this inference is not valid: a function can have points of continuity even when all of its nontrivial difference operators are nowhere continuous. This leaves “open” (for me at least) the question of just how large the set of continuity points can be under these conditions. We formalize this in the next exercises and questions.

[Edit, 04/04/26: I have since found some partial answers to the questions of size of the set of continuity points; namely the Baire Category Theorem forces these sets to be nowhere dense. See the appendix below.]

Let denote the set of points of continuity of a function .

Exercises.

  1. Let be a periodic function and suppose there is a such that is a nonzero constant. Show that must be unbounded on every open interval, and show this forces . (Hint: justify the assertion that, for such a , . Then argue that must be dense, and use this to show that is nowhere bounded)
  2. Find a periodic function with nonempty such that is nowhere continuous for all . Conclude that the argument used in Theorem 1 does not directly generalize to all functions with nonempty . (Hint: constructing so that coincides with makes things simpler, though note this is not necessary.)

And lastly, the questions which I don’t know how to answer, and whose answers I was not able to find after a bit of searching on the internet:

[Edit, 04/04/26: keep reading to the appendix below for partial answers.]

“Open” questions.

  1. When the conditions of Exercise 2 above are met, how large can be (can it be uncountable? can it have nonzero measure?) What other properties could have? It turns out it must be nowhere dense and thus topologically quite “small”; see the appendix.
  2. Is it possible to find a non-constant periodic function with nonempty such that contains two incommensurable periods for some ? How about for all ? In either situation, how large can be, in the various senses above?
  3. Does Theorem 1 still hold if “continuous” is replaced by “having at least one point of continuity”? In other words, if and are incommensurable periodic functions and at least one of them (say ) has a nonempty set of continuity points, must fail to be periodic? And if it does not hold, what is the weakest continuity condition on that still forces commensurability to be necessary for to be periodic? See the appendix for two theorems, Theorem 2 and Theorem 3, which strengthen Theorem 1 and thus partially answer this question.

I plan to come back to this in a future post, and would be glad to hear from any readers who have ideas on answers to these questions.

Beyond Continuity: A Preview of Pathology

The above discussion shows that continuity acts as a rigid cage, forcing period groups in the non-constant case to be cyclic, and in particular nowhere dense, while also preventing sums of incommensurable functions from being periodic. In fact, as discussed in the appendix, even a “small” set of continuity points is enough to force these restrictions.

This means any periodic functions with dense period groups and any pair of incommensurable functions whose sum manages to remain periodic must be fairly pathological, at least from the point of view of their pointwise behavior. Namely, their sets of continuity points are nowhere dense, most (perhaps all?) such functions are actually nowhere continuous, and many are even nowhere bounded.

In later installments of Pathological Periodicity, we will explore these examples more closely, including some highly unintuitive functions found using the Axiom of Choice.

Appendix: The Baire Category Theorem and the Size of Sets of Continuity Points

Originally, I had formulated the “open” questions mostly in terms of density (can be dense, or somewhere dense, while is nowhere continuous for all or at least some ?). Once again displaying my rustiness, a bit more searching revealed that none of these sets of continuity points can be dense, by the Baire Category Theorem. And in fact, under the conditions most relevant to an attempt to strengthen Theorem 1, they must be nowhere dense.

I will assume some basic familiarity with topology, but to clarify notation and terminology: the closure of a subset of a topological space we will denote by , and the interior by . If there is no ambiguity about the underlying topological space we are working with, we drop the subscripts and simply write , etc. We say is somewhere dense if . Otherwise, it is nowhere dense.

The above definition for somewhere density is equivalent to the requirement that there be some nonempty open set such that is a dense subspace of when is equipped with the subspace topology; i.e., if . The reader can verify that the second equality holds for open subsets .

The main point of this appendix is to show the following:

Theorem 2 Let be a periodic function such that is a somewhere dense subset of , and let be any other periodic function. Then is periodic if and only if are commensurable.

A Baire space is any topological space in which the intersection of countably many dense open sets is dense. The Baire Category Theorem states that any complete metric space (like ) is a Baire space. I had embarrassingly forgotten this theorem and the fact that, for any function , the set of continuity points is always a set — an intersection of countably many open sets.

The implications of the Baire category theorem are most apparent if we first analyze the case where is dense (its closure is all of ), not just somewhere dense. In this case, it is necessarily the case that the set is also a dense for any , and thus by Baire, the intersection must also be dense. But this intersection is contained in , since is continuous at any point where both and are continuous. Thus, if is dense, then must be dense as well for any and all , and thus can never be nowhere continuous. This shows that the conditions of Exercise 2 above cannot be met when is dense.

Combining this with Exercise 1, we get that if are incommensurable periodic functions such that is dense, then cannot be periodic. But Theorem 2 states that this is true not just for dense but for somewhere dense , which is a strictly weaker condition. Extending to this weaker condition is not very difficult but it is also not entirely automatic: unlike the case for “absolute” density, if is only somewhere dense, then there can exist many such that is nowhere continuous. In other words, when we relax the conditions of Exercise 2 to only require some (rather than all) to have nowhere continuous, we can find examples whose points of continuity are in fact equal to a union of open intervals:

Example 1 Define on by on and on , then extend to all of with period . Then is strictly periodic, and , which is a union of open intervals and is therefore somewhere dense. For any with , the translate is disjoint from , and one can verify that is nowhere continuous.

To extend the Baire argument to the somewhere dense case, the key is the following lemma.

Lemma 1 Suppose is periodic and is somewhere dense. Then for any , there exists a nonzero integer such that is nonempty, and in fact somewhere dense.

Proof. First, a somewhere dense set is in particular nonempty, so has at least one point of continuity. By Proposition 1, either is constant or is not dense. If is constant, then for every , and there is nothing to prove. Otherwise is not dense, so by Proposition 2 is strictly periodic, and by Fact 2 we have , where is the fundamental period of . We fix this for the rest of the proof.

If , we are done: there is a nonzero integer with , so is a period of and is continuous everywhere.

Suppose then that and are incommensurable. The basic strategy is to find so that the closures of and intersect in a set with nonempty interior; in other words, we want both of these sets to be dense with respect to a nonempty open subset of equipped with the subspace topology.

First observe that for any period , we have , and so actually . This is because a sequence converges to if and only if the sequence converges to , and since is a period, meaning that if and only if , and thus is a point of continuity if and only if is.

The -invariance of naturally extends both to its closure and to the interior of its closure (as the reader can verify). Say ; by hypothesis, this is a nonempty open set in . Therefore we can find an open interval , and every translate with is also a subset of .

Next, since and are incommensurable, the subgroup is dense in by Corollary 2. In fact so is , because is closed with empty interior: for any nonempty open , the set is still open and nonempty, hence meets , and the points where it does lie in . Every element of this set has the form with , since would put it in .

So fix . By the density just established, there are integers and with . The intervals and have the same length , and their left endpoints differ by , so they overlap. Hence is open and nonempty.

To clean up notation, let’s write and . Observe that , so . In particular, and . This of course tells us and . So, using openness of , we obtain

In other words, both and are dense subsets of when equipped with the subspace topology. Moreover, they are both sets in the topology of . But is a Baire space, since it is an open subspace of a Baire space, meaning that we must conclude that is dense in , i.e., is somewhere dense (and nonempty).

As before, however, so we have finished the proof.

Theorem 2 then follows immediately from this lemma and the following theorem, which itself follows from Exercise 1:

Theorem 3 Suppose is a periodic function that is bounded in at least one interval, and such that for at least one nonzero . Then, for any with period , is periodic if and only if are commensurable.

Proof. The proof follows the same structure as that of Theorem 1. If are incommensurable and is periodic, then for any nonzero , the function is nonzero and has a dense period group (because in this case its period group is given by Equation 2) and is thus either nowhere continuous or a nonzero constant. Under our hypothesis, there is one such such that has points of continuity, and must therefore be a nonzero constant. But Exercise 1 shows is nowhere bounded, a contradiction. Thus cannot be incommensurable under our hypotheses.

Whether we can strengthen these theorems any further remains “open,” to me at least. Although, as we will see later, there do exist bounded incommensurable periodic functions whose sums are periodic, which significantly limits how much more we can strengthen Theorem 3.

When it comes to this post, often the edits have been mostly cosmetic. But on two occasions I have made substantial revisions worth highlighting since they are part of the “story” of how this post has come together. The first was the appendix, which I added on 4/04/26. Then on 10/31/26 I looked back at it and found myself distinctly dissatisfied. So, I rewrote a good chunk of it to make it somewhat more detailed and rigorous; the underlying ideas didn’t change, but it is now I hope clearer (and free of sign errors). I then also significantly rewrote the introduction in ways that impact the overall presentation of the material. In particular, earlier versions leaned on the notion of the rank of a subgroup of the reals, which coincides with the dimension of the -vector subspace spanned by . I used rank as an indicator of whether the group is dense (if rank , then it is dense, though converse doesn’t hold), and so I used it in discussing strict periodicity. But this is clunky for various reasons, not least of which is that actually these notions of rank and dimension do not quite work in most choiceless models of ZF (models where the axiom of choice as such fails even if perhaps some consequences of it do still hold). More exactly, in any model without a Hamel basis, an arbitrary -subspace of that isn’t finite dimensional might not have a well defined dimension at all. So the corresponding notion of rank also falls apart in those cases. A big part of the raison d’être for this series is to investigate what results about periodicity and periodic decomposition survive in choiceless set theories, so it seemed best to part with this notion for now. I will return to a discussion of rank and dimension in a separate post.↩︎

item.title: Pathological Periodicity, Part I: Relearning the Basics
item.dc:creator: Alonso Espinosa Domínguez
item.description:
This is Part I of the series Pathological Periodicity.

Let me begin with a more narrative introduction to this series, which will be followed by a more technical one in the next post.

My hiatus from math has been quite long. It’s been 9 years since my last algebra class (algebra was one of my weaker subjects, and I regrettably avoided it in favor of taking more analysis classes), a little under 8 years since I seriously attempted any research, 7 years since I gave up on becoming a mathematician, and 6 years since my last math class whatsoever. Needless to say, I am exceedingly rusty. So when life pushed me to reconsider my divorce from mathematics, I thought to myself, let me revisit the basics. And hence I picked up Axler’s excellent Linear Algebra Done Right and began working through the exercises, to start getting the wheels turning again.

Just in the first chapter, I came across a very innocent-seeming question. Is the set of all periodic functions a vector subspace of , the space of all real-valued functions on ? As rusty as I may be, I was still able to quickly and emphatically answer in the negative. Though sums of functions with commensurable periods are always periodic, obviously sums of periodic functions with incommensurable periods (i.e., periods whose ratio is irrational) surely fail to be periodic. Moreover, the only possible vector subspaces consisting solely of periodic functions would definitely have to be made up of functions whose periods are commensurable with one another. I thought to myself, I will hammer out a quick little proof of this, and I will move on to more exciting things in linear algebra.

And then I sat down to write and found myself a little bit…stuck. First, I realized I needed to be a bit more precise with what I meant by functions having incommensurable periods. I didn’t just need there to exist periods of and of with , I needed all periods of to be incommensurable with those of in order for to potentially fail to be periodic. This was important to specify because constant functions have the “unusual” property of having incommensurable real numbers in their sets of periods, since their set of periods is just all of , and this is what makes it possible to add them to any periodic function without affecting the periodicity at all.

So now I had two questions at once on my mind:

  • Question 1: Was I wrong about sums of incommensurable functions? That is, can I find a pair of such that they are incommensurable in the sense that they have no periods in common (equivalent to having no periods that are rational multiples of each other) and yet is periodic?
  • Question 2: Are there any functions other than constant functions that can have two or more incommensurable periods?

For a brief period (pun intended) of time, I continued believing that the answer to the above would be no. In particular, for the second question, I realized that if a set of periods contains incommensurables, it would have to be dense. And surely, only constant functions could have a dense set of periods, right?

With a little more thought, I concluded this is not hard to prove if I restrict myself to continuous functions…and that the proof for continuous functions cannot really be generalized to all functions. This was precisely the moment I realized I was almost certainly wrong about Question 2, and by extension probably wrong about Question 1 as well. Even the better part of a decade later, I still remember vividly just how pathological a function can get when you abandon continuity. All of a sudden, the prospect of a non-constant function with a dense set of periods seemed like exactly the sort of thing possible in the strange world of nowhere continuous functions.

So I set out to come up with some examples. Within hours, I had my first example showing Question 2 could be answered affirmatively: if I chose any incommensurable , then the characteristic function over would be non-constant and have a set of periods equal to all of .

Question 1 proved to be a bit trickier for me, but after a day or two, I finally came up with an example also answering this question affirmatively. I will discuss this and other examples later; for now I will give any readers a chance to try to come up with examples themselves. Suffice it to say, I was extremely intrigued. And as soon as I answered one question, more questions arose. For instance:

  • Question 3: Now that I know sums of incommensurable functions do not always fail to be periodic, is there a neat characterization of when these sums end up being periodic?
  • Question 4: Can I find a vector subspace of that consists solely of periodic functions and yet contains two or more incommensurable functions?
  • Question 5: All the examples I had at that point for both Questions 1 and 2 were constant almost everywhere. Do there exist examples that aren’t? Can I find examples that are constant “almost nowhere”? Would these examples have to be non-measurable?
  • Question 6: Clearly, sets of periods can have some interesting topological and algebraic structure. Sometimes they are dense, and they are always at least an additive group. Sometimes, they are also a vector space over . What more can be said about these groups/spaces of periods and how they determine the behavior of the function they arise from?

I can genuinely say, I had not felt this excited about math in at least 8 years. My excitement multiplied even more when I noticed I could invoke the Axiom of Choice to answer Questions 4 and 5 affirmatively as well (except for the measurability part). [Edit: actually I am pretty sure now that I was wrong about Question 4, though it is not so hard to prove without AC that there are at least -vector spaces generated by periodic functions with incommensurable periods. See future posts]. [Edit2 (04-29-2026): Nevermind! This, and much more, is indeed possible with the axiom of choice].

In other words, here I was, thinking I was just doing a rudimentary exercise in Chapter 1 of a linear algebra text, only to open a can of worms involving many fields of mathematics at once: algebra, measure theory, topology, and set theory.

With a little digging, I learned that unsurprisingly many others have been interested in similar questions. There is, in fact, a substantial body of work on what is called the Periodic Decomposition Problem, which takes many of the questions I had been posing in directions I had not yet imagined (see for instance this survey paper).

I have much more to learn about the work done so far on the Periodic Decomposition Problem. But I do think I have identified some aspects of this problem that haven’t been directly tackled in the literature so far. Let me explain: basically the whole line of enquiry in Pathological Periodicity is about functions that admit periodic decompositions where and are incommensurable with each other (and thus with their sum). One of the questions that seems to be unaddressed is about the axiomatics of periodic decompositions, and in particular of incommensurable decompositions of functions that are already periodic (a decomposition of an already periodic function into two or more periodic functions will naturally often fail to be an incommensurable decomposition). ZF alone is enough to prove that functions with periodic decompositions exist, but the only periodic ones that can be proven to decompose incommensurably in ZF are a.e. constant. Whats more, in ZF alone, it doesn’t seem so possible to find conditions on that are sufficient to guarantee it has a decomposition. On the other hand, in ZFC, there is a very simple necesarry and sufficient condition on any that determines whether it has a periodic decomposition. As I will show later on in the series, this condition also holds for the “stronger” variant of the problem requiring incommensurability of the summands in the decomposition. Moreover, ZFC abounds with examples of decomposable functions that are not constant a.e., and non-measurable. So, this has led me to wonder which axiom systems “between” ZF and ZFC still allow for the existence of these nonmeasurbale examples, which ones allow for a full solution of the decomposition problem and its “stronger” variant, and whether the classical and the incommensurable variants can be separated from each other by the strength of the axioms needed to prove them (and thus if we can be truly justified in calling the incommensurable variant “stronger” than the original). In other words, I want to figure out the precise “heirarchy” of axioms needed to prove the various versions of the periodic decomposition problem, and to understand how the properties of the functions involved in the decomposition relate to the strength of the axioms needed to prove their existence.

While I work on these questions (and write up the results more formally), I want to use this blog to bring any readers along with me on this journey into the world of Pathological Periodicity. I hope you enjoy it as much as I have. See you in the next post!

Up next: Part II: The Cage of Continuity →

item.title: Returning, Not Repeating
item.dc:creator: Alonso Espinosa Domínguez
item.description:
Despite a couple of terrible math teachers I had early in middle school (the kind that cause most people to loathe math for the rest of their lives), by the end I still fell in love with the subject. From that point forward, I spent much of my time chaotically pursuing anything and everything that caught my eye mathematically. I got an intoxicating taste of the awesome experience of forming a conjecture and then, after pondering over it for days or weeks, finally proving it wrong or right. I went on to major in math during college at MIT, engaged in a few attempted research projects (one of which eventually led to a joint publication), and graduated with a math degree in 2020. I then stopped doing math for a few years.

My departure from the subject was not precisely graceful. By the time I graduated, I was, I guess you could say, rather “burnt out”. For sure, much of that exhaustion was self-inflicted. For instance, taking a graduate-level measure theory course my freshman spring was, in retrospect, not the wisest decision. My brash, impatient impulse to advance as fast as possible in the topics that interested me while skipping over everything else shot me in the foot over and over again while in college. Each time, I managed not to learn the appropriate lesson.

This is perhaps not too surprising, given the fact that I had been using math as a kind of crutch. Like many in our messed-up capitalist society, I have had my share of struggles with anxiety, depression, and the like. In the years before falling in love with math, these struggles were particularly acute and characterized by a profound sense of purposelessness. Discovering at age 13 or so that I really liked math and that, with sufficient tenacity, I could advance considerably beyond the standard school curriculum gave me a sense of purpose and self-worth. Not to mention, it also provided an escape from problems in my life and in the world around me.

Inevitably this dynamic began to eat away at the joy of engaging in the difficult struggle of learning math and (later on) of carrying out research. Math is hard, and it is hard for everyone. “There is no royal road to geometry,” as Euclid reportedly said, nor is there one to science in general as Marx later added. But when “success” in math (or any other pursuit) becomes a substitute for a sense of self-worth, the challenges and failures one comes up against can easily become supposed signs of irremediable inadequacy. This frame of mind naturally also facilitates falling into a frankly silly competitive dynamic. For some of us in college, for instance, the number of grad classes we took as undergrads became a ridiculous metric by which we judged our future prospects. The result was to render the tortuous path of learning and discovery into a torturous one that ceases to actually be primarily about learning or discovery.

The consequences of the aforementioned mistakes in my approach were certainly a major contributing factor to my lengthy departure from math. They were far from the only factor, however. In parallel to my “burnout,” I was also increasingly drawn to struggles against various outrages in society. From cozying up to Mohammed bin Salman while he was the lead architect of the atrocious US-armed Saudi war against Yemen, to establishing ties with Jeffrey Epstein, and much more, MIT provided no shortage of examples to fight against.

So, as I started moving away from math, I didn’t take any time to rest, or to reflect terribly much on my time doing mathematics. Instead, I threw myself into organizing: first at MIT, and then amongst public housing tenants, at my unionized workplace, and elsewhere. I read up on Marxism, history, some philosophy, and generally spent a lot of time thinking a lot about the material forces shaping society in a way I had not quite done before. This changed my worldview considerably; unsurprisingly, it also thoroughly changed how I see mathematics.

Up until around halfway through college, my view of the subject and of reality more generally was vaguely Kantian. Teenage me became convinced that whatever objective reality (the realm of “things in themselves”) might be, we couldn’t truly know anything about it. The only knowledge I thought we could form from the “chaotic diversity of our sense experience”1 with this reality was knowledge about ourselves, i.e. about how we experience things, whilst the things themselves remained fundamentally out of reach. Science, I thought, was the process of imposing structure on this chaotic diversity so as to make it amenable to a coherent system of thought, and nothing more. Since the most definite and coherent systems of thought were mathematical, mathematics seemed to me a study of the finest and most powerful structures the mind has for arriving at the only kind of knowledge it can form.

I started seriously questioning this view just before I fully threw myself into politics and activism, largely because of how incompatible it is with the jarring concreteness of social and political life. If the structures of the mind are what matter most, then what do I make of the fact that people face material oppression and exploitation right now, in ways that have nothing to do with mental structures? (at least not in the sense I had been thinking about “mental structures”).

All these years later, by no means have I arrived at anything like a worked-out philosophy of math or of anything else. But if I had to roughly summarize the basic suppositions which I now take as a starting point, they would include:

  1. there is a real, objective, material world;
  2. we represent it mentally and symbolically;
  3. our representations improve precisely through the process of acting in the world and confronting the consequences;
  4. this process results in direct, albeit partial, knowledge of reality.

From this vantage point, mathematics looks rather different. The objects of mathematics – numbers, relations, structures, sets, categories, so on – are not constructs of the mind projecting itself outward to generate the only domain we can form knowledge of. On the contrary, they are real features of material reality that we have learned, over the course of millennia, to perceive, abstract, and reason about. And we have learned to do so by actively intervening (or perhaps the better word is laboring) to transform this material reality in pursuit of variety of largely socially-determined ends. Just think of the role of land surveying in the history of the emergence of geometry.

This shift in perspective helped me reopen the door to the world of mathematics; mathematics’ wonders have done the rest of the work needed to draw me back in fully.

And so, Mathematical Adventures is, first of all, an attempt to actually do mathematics again, and to do so in an adventurous spirit. After all these years, I am certainly rusty, and I need a good deal of practice thinking about and writing mathematics. This will include posing a ton of mathematical questions and documenting the messy process of trying to answer them. But I also intend to make it a place for the kind of meta-mathematical reflection I have hinted at here. So, expect to see some explorations into the philosophy of math, its history, its relationship to other sciences, and its relationship to our class-divided society at large.

The first series, Pathological Periodicity, is squarely in the first category2 — a deep dive into the surprisingly rich world of periodic functions that began with a single exercise in Chapter 1 of a linear algebra textbook. Later posts will venture further into the second.
